newsitem.title: USA: BPA sees near-record 1997 Snake River runoff.
newsitem.headline: BPA sees near-record 1997 Snake River runoff.

text.p: The Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) projects 1997 runoff on the Snake River to be near record levels, while runoff on the Columbia River will be in the top 10 percent of the historical record, the agency said in a letter to an Oregon state Senator dated Wednesday.
"The volume of water this spring will completely overwhelm the hydraulic capacity of the generating system, even when all turbines are on-line and running flat-out," BPA said.
The Snake River, which runs west from the Rocky Mountains across Idaho, is a major tributary of the Columbia.

The agency, responding to the Senator's concerns about migration of endangered fish species, said "overgeneration spill" will elevate dissolved gas levels (which are harmful to fish), but by fewer than five percentage points.
Overgeneration spill refers to water that could have been passed through turbines if there were demand for the resulting power, a situation which occurs at nighttime and weekends.
Increased gas levels are also caused by "lack-of-turbine" spill and BPA said it is working with the U.S. Army Corps to maximize turbine availability this spring.
All but five units at the lower Snake/Columbia River dams are expected to be available for service, compared with about 10 units out of service during the 1996 spring migration, BPA said.
The other main strategy for reducing lack-of-turbine spill is to maximize storage of water in reservoirs during the runoff.

"This year, virtually every storage reservoir on the system will be drawn down as much as possible prior to the spring freshet for flood control, allowing as much spring runoff to be stored as possible," BPA said.

Other actions to reduce spill include shutting down the 1,158 megawatt (MW) Washington Nuclear Plant prior to the migration season and not restarting it until dissolved gas is below certain levels and energy from the plant can be marketed.

BPA said it was "aggressively marketing our expected surplus energy inventory," which it estimates at 5,000 to 6,000 average megawatt hours of uncommitted light-load hour energy in the April to June period.
"Our uncommitted heavy load hour inventory is much less, and we are able to market virtually all of it either on an advance contract basis or through the daily spot market," BPA said.

BPA said its spring marketing strategy includes discount pricing for flat and light load hour products; aggressive pursuance of thermal displacement sales; negotiation of an energy exchange with Alberta's Transalta Utility Corp; and sales of a light load hour product that allows the buyer to distinguish higher valued light load hours.
